clue.text: Teller, rather than ordinary accountant.

parts.note: a teller is usually a bank clerk who counts money; here it is one who tells, spreading gossip and secrets

explanation.walkthrough: A bank teller handles accounts, so 'Teller' points at money; the clue says this teller tells tales instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A tattletale is a gossip or informer, someone who tells on others rather than counting cash.

clue.text: Road out? Rub the wrong way and this oldster could have given you the air.

definitions.text: this oldster could have given you the air

indicators.note: taken in the wrong order, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A road out, rubbed up the wrong way, and an old-timer who might have sent you packing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The wrong way' tells you to rearrange ROAD OUT plus RUB. 'Given you the air' suggests dismissing someone, but an air is a melody.
explanation.definitionFit: A troubadour was a medieval travelling poet-singer, someone from long ago who sang songs.

clue.text: Reputedly company that could be on course.

definitions.text: Reputedly company that could be on course.

parts.words: Reputedly company that could be on course.
parts.note: the saying 'two's company'; a pair playing a golf course together

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'two's company, three's a crowd' says a pair is company, and a pair playing golf is a recognised format.
explanation.definitionFit: A twosome is a pair of people, including two golfers going round a course together.

clue.text: One with such would appreciate half fare at most.

definitions.text: One with such would appreciate half fare at most.

parts.words: One with such would appreciate half fare at most.
parts.note: 'fare' sounds like a ticket price but means food; someone off their food wants half a portion

explanation.walkthrough: Half fare suggests a cheap ticket; here fare is food, and someone with no hunger would want only a small helping.
explanation.definitionFit: Loss of appetite is a lack of desire to eat, so a person with it would welcome only a little food.

clue.text: With 3, one might not be by food.

definitions.text: With 3, one might not be by food.

parts.words: With 3, one might not be by food.
parts.note: someone with a loss of appetite (3 down) would not be enticed by food; the answer fills the gap after 'be'

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a sentence with the answer missing after 'be': someone off their food might not be lured by it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempted means enticed or lured, as a hungry person is by the sight of food.

clue.text: Prepared to fire, with it being commonly drunk.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a gun with a cartridge in it is ready to shoot
second meaning: in slang, heavily intoxicated

explanation.walkthrough: 'Commonly' marks the drunk sense as slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A loaded gun has ammunition in it, and slang uses the same word for someone thoroughly intoxicated.

clue.text: An unspecified person's comment on Mr. World?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: someone or other, a person not named
second meaning: read as two words, '...!' is what you might exclaim at a bodybuilding champion

explanation.walkthrough: Mr. World is a bodybuilding title, so the admiring remark about the winner's physique splits the answer as SOME BODY.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody is the everyday pronoun for a person left unnamed, as in 'somebody called'.

clue.text: His hair might be white or red, lost in the shuffle.

definitions.note: the answer is a person, and grey or white hair marks age

indicators.note: mixed up as cards are, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man's hair colour, white or red, gets mislaid in a reshuffle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'White or red' reads as a choice of hair colour; only 'red' and 'lost' are the letters that 'in the shuffle' tells you to mix.
explanation.definitionFit: An oldster is an elderly person, typically one with white hair.

clue.text: When short of funds, they might have no meeting.

definitions.text: When short of funds, they might have no meeting.

parts.words: When short of funds, they might have no meeting.
parts.note: the idiom about scraping by on one's income says these must meet; when broke they fail to

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a committee cancelling a meeting for lack of money, but it plays on 'making ends meet'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'make ends meet' means to have just enough income for expenses.

clue.text: Such pictures might try to extol the virtues of application.

definitions.text: Such pictures might try to extol the virtues of application.

parts.words: Such pictures might try to extol the virtues of application.
parts.note: 'application' sounds like hard work but means applying a product, shown in two contrasting photographs

explanation.walkthrough: 'Application' suggests diligence; the pictures show the state before and after a product, such as a cream or paint, is applied.
explanation.definitionFit: Advertisers use paired before-and-after photographs to show the improvement a product brings.

clue.text: One familiarly said to be a dead player.

definitions.text: One familiarly said to be a dead player.

parts.words: One familiarly said to be a dead player.
parts.note: the animal's familiar short name appears in the idiom for pretending to be dead

explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing possum' means feigning death, and possum is the familiar form of the animal's full name.
explanation.definitionFit: The opossum is the marsupial famous for going limp and appearing lifeless when threatened.

clue.text: It seems to be about noon, with some possible alterations.

definitions.text: It seems to be about noon
definitions.meaning: first meaning: read as ..., the morning is over, so it must be around noon
second meaning: changed or revised in places

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as A.M. + ENDED: once the morning has ended it is about noon.
explanation.definitionFit: An amended text or law is one that has been revised, with changes made to it.

clue.text: The volume of its members changes periodically.

definitions.text: The volume of its members changes periodically.

parts.words: The volume of its members changes periodically.
parts.note: 'volume' sounds like loudness but means a book; the members receive a different book each month

explanation.walkthrough: 'Volume' suggests noise and 'members' a body of people getting louder; the volume is the book the club's members are sent, and it changes every month.
explanation.definitionFit: The Book-of-the-Month Club was a famous American mail-order service sending subscribers a selected title monthly.

clue.text: Old people got so short-changed!

definitions.note: the answer is an ancient people, plural

indicators.note: the letters are altered into a fresh order

explanation.surface: Elderly folk complain they have been short-changed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short-changed' hides the fodder word 'short' and the signal 'changed'; 'Old people' sounds like pensioners but means a historic nation.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ostrogoths were an ancient Germanic people who ruled Italy in the sixth century.

clue.text: You might find this dish dear, but the result would be persistent.

definitions.note: the answer is a plural noun, persistent people who refuse to give up

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are reworked and what comes out is something else

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A diner spots an expensive dish on the menu and reckons the consequence would linger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You might find this' leads into the letters of 'dish dear'; 'but the result would be' says that what they make, rearranged, is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Diehards are stubborn people who resist change to the last, the persistent ones.

clue.text: What is left when one who comes out has the title backwards.

parts.note: a deb, short for debutante, is a young woman who 'comes out' into society

indicators.note: the title is to be read in reverse order

parts.note: Sir is the title given to a knight

explanation.surface: A debutante's title gets turned the wrong way round, and something is left over.
explanation.definitionFit: Debris is the scattered remains or rubble left behind after something is destroyed.

clue.text: One takes his hat off this way when one of the last of the tribe goes soft inside.

definitions.text: takes his hat off this way
definitions.note: the answer is a verb in the third person, matching 'takes', with 'this way' pointing to the manner named by the answer

indicators.note: the soft letter is placed within the Mohican's name

parts.words: one of the last of the tribe
parts.note: Uncas is a character in James Fenimore Cooper's novel The Last of the Mohicans
p (piano) is the musical marking for soft

explanation.surface: A tribesman removes his hat as a member of a dying tribe grows gentle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The last of the tribe' looks like a final letter, but it nods to The Last of the Mohicans, whose hero Uncas is meant; 'inside' puts P within his name.
explanation.definitionFit: To uncap is to remove a cap, so a man doffing his cap is uncapping.

clue.text: What people believe around the early hours should be smoothed out.

indicators.note: the belief wraps round the early hours

parts.note: a creed is a set of beliefs
a.m. denotes the hours after midnight

explanation.surface: Beliefs held in the small hours ought to be ironed out.
explanation.definitionFit: In cooking, creamed butter or potatoes have been beaten until smooth and lump-free.

clue.text: One shouldn't miss this broadside.

parts.note: 'broadside' suggests a cannon volley but means the wide flat side of a farm building

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom says a poor shot 'couldn't hit the broad side of a barn', so this is the target nobody should miss.
explanation.definitionFit: A barn door is proverbially the largest, easiest target, hence 'as big as a barn door'.

clue.text: Stuck with the problem of finding her dead?

indicators.note: a puzzle to be worked out, so the letters must be sorted into a new order

explanation.surface: A detective stuck with the case of finding a woman dead.
explanation.definitionFit: Adhered means clung or stuck fast to something.

clue.text: Perform an elemental operation on an animal at one time, possibly.

parts.note: an ox is a bovine animal
I is the Roman numeral for one
a date is a point in time

explanation.surface: A chemist tries something elemental on an animal at some past time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At one time' reads as 'formerly', but it splits into one (I) and time (DATE).
explanation.definitionFit: To oxidate is to combine with oxygen, a chemical element, hence an elemental operation.

clue.text: The place of control, reputedly, might be either English or Western.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: someone in charge is 'in the ...'

definitions.text: might be either English or Western
definitions.meaning: second meaning: English and Western are the two main styles of riding seat

explanation.walkthrough: 'English or Western' sounds like a choice of nationality, but they are two kinds of riding equipment.
explanation.definitionFit: A rider sits on a saddle, and being 'in the saddle' is an idiom for holding command.

clue.text: Implying the heart of fire we used to say the English lacked.

definitions.text: Implying the heart of fire we used to say the English lacked.

parts.words: Implying the heart of fire we used to say the English lacked.
parts.note: 'heart of fire' sounds like passion, which the English were said to lack; it is heat supplied from a central source

explanation.walkthrough: The English were stereotyped as lacking fire in the heart, but the American joke was that English houses lacked heat from a central boiler.
explanation.definitionFit: Central heating warms a whole building from one furnace, which old British homes famously went without.

clue.text: See 12
Not an express hampering of movement if you are.

definitions.text: Not an express hampering of movement if you are.

parts.words: Not an express hampering of movement if you are.
parts.note: read the answer after 'if you are': being restricted hampers your movement, so you are no express

explanation.walkthrough: The answer completes 'if you are ...': someone restricted moves slowly, unlike an express. 'Express' sets up a train, and the answer is also a word railways have used in train names.
explanation.definitionFit: Limited means restricted or confined, as anyone whose movement is hampered is.

clue.text: Take something back about the document.

parts.note: re means about or concerning
a tract is a short written treatise or pamphlet

explanation.surface: Someone takes back a statement about a document.
explanation.definitionFit: To retract is to withdraw a statement or claim, taking back what was said.

clue.text: See 6
When butchered, sells a deer without a head.

indicators.note: cut up like a carcass, so these letters are hacked about into a new order

explanation.surface: A butcher sells a deer carcass with its head removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butchered' tells you to cut up SELLS A DEER. 'Without a head' looks like an instruction to drop a first letter, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A leaderless group has no one at its head, no chief to direct it.
